WITH ranked_employees AS (
    SELECT
        e.name AS employee_name,
        e.salary,
        e.department_id,
        RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.department_id ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS salary_rank
    FROM employees e
)
SELECT
    d.name AS department_name,
    re.employee_name,
    re.salary,
    re.salary_rank
FROM ranked_employees re
JOIN departments d ON re.department_id = d.id
WHERE re.salary_rank <= 3
ORDER BY d.name, re.salary_rank;

## Identity and Access Management

Identity and Access Management (IAM) forms the cornerstone of any robust cybersecurity framework. At its core, IAM ensures that the right individuals have access to the right resources at the right times and for the right reasons. This discipline encompasses the policies, technologies, and processes that govern digital identities and their associated permissions. Organizations that neglect IAM fundamentals inevitably face heightened risks of credential theft, privilege escalation, and unauthorized data exposure. The principle of least privilege—granting users only the permissions strictly necessary to perform their duties—must be enforced rigorously across all systems, from cloud infrastructure to on-premises legacy applications.

Multi-factor authentication (MFA) represents one of the single most impactful controls an organization can deploy. By requiring two or more verification factors—something you know, something you have, or something you are—MFA dramatically reduces the success rate of credential-based attacks. Modern implementations increasingly favor phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO2 security keys and device-bound biometrics over SMS-based one-time codes, which remain vulnerable to SIM-swapping and interception. Organizations should prioritize MFA enrollment for all user populations, with particular urgency for administrators, executives, and anyone with access to sensitive financial or personal data. Conditional access policies that evaluate contextual signals such as device health, geolocation, and sign-in risk further strengthen the authentication layer.

Privileged access management (PAM) deserves dedicated attention separate from general IAM controls. Privileged accounts—whether belonging to system administrators, database owners, or service principals—represent the most valuable targets for adversaries. A comprehensive PAM strategy incorporates just-in-time access provisioning, session monitoring and recording, credential vaulting with automatic rotation, and the elimination of standing privileges wherever feasible. Organizations should also implement break-glass procedures that balance emergency access requirements with appropriate security controls, ensuring that crisis scenarios do not become vectors for abuse. Regular access reviews and entitlement certifications close the loop, preventing the gradual accumulation of unnecessary permissions that so often accompanies organizational change.

## Network Defense and Segmentation

Network defense begins with the fundamental recognition that perimeter-based security models are insufficient in modern, distributed environments. The zero trust architecture model, predicated on the principle of "never trust, always verify," has emerged as the guiding philosophy for contemporary network design. Under this paradigm, every access request is authenticated, authorized, and encrypted regardless of its origin, and implicit trust is never granted based solely on network location. Micro-segmentation techniques allow organizations to divide their networks into granular security zones, constraining lateral movement even after an initial compromise occurs. This approach requires deep visibility into east-west traffic patterns and the discipline to maintain segmentation policies as applications evolve.

Firewall configuration management demands ongoing vigilance and periodic auditing. Next-generation firewalls (NGFWs) provide application-layer inspection, intrusion prevention, and threat intelligence integration that far surpass the capabilities of traditional stateful packet filters. However, these advanced features deliver value only when properly configured and maintained. Rule sprawl—the accumulation of overly permissive, redundant, or obsolete firewall rules—creates attack surface that adversaries eagerly exploit. Organizations should enforce a rigorous change management process for firewall modifications, conduct quarterly rule reviews, and employ automated policy analysis tools to detect anomalies such as any-to-any rules, expired temporary exceptions, and shadowed rules that mask the true effective policy.

Network detection and response (NDR) capabilities complement preventive controls by identifying threats that bypass perimeter defenses. Deploying strategically placed sensors that analyze network traffic metadata enables security teams to detect command-and-control communications, data exfiltration attempts, and reconnaissance activities. The integration of network telemetry with endpoint and identity data through a security information and event management (SIEM) or extended detection and response (XDR) platform provides the correlated visibility necessary for rapid threat hunting and investigation. Organizations should also maintain comprehensive network architecture diagrams, asset inventories, and data flow maps, as these artifacts prove invaluable during incident response and forensic analysis exercises.

## Endpoint and Data Protection

Endpoint security has evolved far beyond traditional signature-based antivirus toward integrated platforms that combine prevention, detection, and response capabilities. Endpoint detection and response (EDR) solutions provide continuous monitoring, behavioral analysis, and the ability to isolate compromised devices remotely. These tools generate rich telemetry that enables security analysts to reconstruct attack timelines, identify root causes, and scope the breadth of an intrusion. Organizations must ensure that endpoint agents are deployed universally across workstations, servers, and cloud workloads, with no gaps that adversaries can exploit. Maintaining current operating system and application patches remains essential, as a significant portion of successful attacks continue to exploit known vulnerabilities for which fixes already exist.

Data classification and protection strategies must address information throughout its lifecycle—at rest, in transit, and in use. Organizations should begin by identifying and inventorying their sensitive data assets, including personally identifiable information (PII), intellectual property, financial records, and regulated data subject to frameworks such as GDPR, HIPAA, or PCI DSS. Data loss prevention (DLP) controls can then be applied to monitor and restrict unauthorized data movement across email, cloud storage, removable media, and web channels. Encryption, whether implemented at the file, database, or disk level, provides a critical compensating control. Effective key management practices, including hardware security modules (HSMs) and strict separation of duties for key custodians, prevent encryption from becoming a false sense of security.

Backup and recovery capabilities represent the ultimate defense against ransomware and destructive attacks. The industry-standard 3-2-1 backup rule—maintaining three copies of data on two different media types, with one copy stored offsite—provides a baseline for resilience. However, modern threats demand additional safeguards: immutable or write-once-read-many (WORM) storage that prevents backup deletion or encryption by attackers, air-gapped copies that are physically or logically isolated from production networks, and regularly tested restoration procedures that validate both the integrity of backups and the organization's ability to recover within acceptable timeframes. Organizations that neglect to test their recovery processes often discover critical gaps only during actual incidents, when time pressure and operational disruption compound the difficulty of restoration.

## Security Operations and Incident Response

A mature security operations function serves as the nervous system of an organization's cybersecurity program. The security operations center (SOC) provides continuous monitoring, threat detection, alert triage, and incident response coordination. Effective SOCs operate with clearly defined tiers of escalation, where tier one analysts handle initial triage, tier two conducts deeper investigation, and tier three engages in threat hunting and advanced forensics. Metrics matter: organizations should track mean time to detect (MTTD), mean time to respond (MTTR), and mean time to contain (MTTC) as key performance indicators, using these measurements to drive continuous improvement rather than assign blame. The adoption of security orchestration, automation, and response (SOAR) platforms helps standardize and accelerate repetitive tasks, reducing analyst burnout and ensuring consistent response quality.

Incident response planning must occur well before the first security event. A documented incident response plan, aligned with frameworks such as NIST SP 800-61 or the SANS PICERL model, provides the structured approach necessary to navigate high-stress situations. The plan should define roles and responsibilities unequivocally, including technical responders, legal counsel, communications teams, and executive leadership. Clear criteria for incident severity classification and escalation prevent the paralysis that occurs when teams cannot distinguish between routine events and genuine crises. Tabletop exercises, where stakeholders walk through simulated scenarios without the pressure of an active incident, build muscle memory and expose gaps in processes, communication channels, or technical capabilities that can be remediated proactively.

Threat intelligence programs enhance both preventive and detective capabilities by contextualizing the threat landscape relevant to the organization's industry, geography, and technology stack. Consuming threat intelligence from commercial providers, open-source feeds, and industry information sharing and analysis centers (ISACs) enables security teams to prioritize vulnerabilities, tune detection rules, and anticipate adversary tactics. Operationalizing threat intelligence means integrating indicators of compromise into security controls automatically and using tactical threat profiles to guide hunting hypotheses. Equally important is the post-incident review process. Every significant security event should generate a blameless retrospective that identifies root causes, documents lessons learned, and produces actionable remediation items tracked to completion through a formal system. This closed-loop learning process distinguishes organizations that genuinely improve their security posture from those that merely survive from one incident to the next.
---FINISH---

## RESTful Resource Modeling

At the heart of any well-designed API lies a coherent resource model that accurately reflects the domain it serves. Resources should represent nouns—tangible entities such as users, orders, or products—rather than actions or procedures. This noun-oriented approach encourages designers to think in terms of the data and its relationships, which naturally maps to the HTTP verbs GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE. By aligning resources with domain concepts, the API becomes intuitive for consumers who already understand the business logic, reducing the cognitive load required to integrate with the system.

Resource granularity is a critical decision that impacts both performance and usability. Resources that are too coarse-grained force clients to fetch excessive data they do not need, inflating bandwidth consumption and slowing response times. Conversely, overly fine-grained resources can lead to the N+1 query problem, where a client must issue dozens or hundreds of requests to assemble a complete view of related data. Striking the right balance often involves providing embedding or expansion parameters that allow clients to request related resources inline, combining the efficiency of coarse-grained responses with the flexibility of fine-grained access patterns.

Relationships between resources deserve careful attention during the modeling phase. Hypermedia links, expressed through standards like HAL or JSON:API, enable discoverability by guiding clients from one resource to related resources without hardcoding URI structures. While not every API must achieve Level 3 on the Richardson Maturity Model, including basic link relations for pagination, parent-child hierarchies, and state transitions dramatically improves the developer experience. A client that receives a collection of orders, each containing a link to its associated customer and line items, can navigate the API graph without consulting external documentation for every endpoint.

Sub-resources and composite identifiers provide a clean mechanism for expressing ownership and scoping. A URI pattern such as `/customers/{customerId}/orders/{orderId}` communicates that an order belongs to a specific customer and cannot exist independently. This nested structure also simplifies authorization logic, as the path itself encodes the scope within which an operation is permitted. Designers should resist the temptation to nest resources too deeply, however; beyond two or three levels, URIs become unwieldy and the parent identifiers can often be inferred from the child resource's own representation.

## Consistency and Predictability

Consistency across an API surface is perhaps the single most impactful factor in determining how quickly developers can adopt and integrate with a service. When every endpoint follows the same naming conventions—using snake_case or camelCase uniformly, employing plural nouns for collections, and applying the same date-time formats—consumers can write client code with confidence, knowing that patterns learned from one endpoint apply everywhere. Inconsistencies, even seemingly minor ones such as mixing `created_at` and `createdAt` within the same payload, force developers to consult documentation repeatedly and write defensive parsing logic that handles multiple variants.

Predictability extends beyond naming to encompass the structure of request and response bodies. Adopting a standardized envelope, such as wrapping all successful responses in an object that contains `data`, `meta`, and `links` keys, gives clients a single parsing strategy that works uniformly. Similarly, establishing conventions for pagination—whether cursor-based for large, frequently updated datasets or offset-based for smaller, stable collections—and applying them without exception prevents the frustration of discovering that one endpoint uses `page` and `size` while another uses `offset` and `limit`. These small frictions accumulate rapidly and erode trust in the API's design quality.

Versioning strategy is an integral component of predictability that must be decided early and enforced rigorously. Whether the version is communicated via a URI path segment, a custom request header, or content negotiation through the Accept header, the chosen approach should remain stable across the API's entire lifespan. Semantic versioning of the API contract, as distinct from the implementation software, helps consumers understand the impact of changes: a minor version addition that introduces new optional fields should never break existing clients, while a major version bump signals the removal or restructuring of existing functionality. Communicating deprecation timelines through response headers like `Sunset` gives consumers the necessary window to migrate.

Idempotency guarantees are another dimension of predictable behavior that API designers must address explicitly. GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS requests are defined as safe and idempotent by the HTTP specification, and PUT and DELETE should be implemented as idempotent operations as well. For POST requests that create resources, providing idempotency keys—unique client-generated tokens that the server uses to deduplicate retried requests—protects against double-creation in the face of network failures. Documenting which operations carry idempotency guarantees and how to leverage them is essential for building resilient integrations that gracefully handle retries and timeouts.

## Error Handling and Feedback

Effective error handling transforms a frustrating debugging session into a clear, actionable experience. Every error response should include at minimum an HTTP status code that accurately reflects the category of problem—4xx for client errors, 5xx for server errors—alongside a machine-readable error code and a human-readable message. The machine-readable code, such as `invalid_payment_method` or `rate_limit_exceeded`, allows client applications to implement conditional logic for handling specific failure modes programmatically, rather than resorting to brittle string parsing of error messages that may change over time.

Structured error bodies should provide sufficient context for diagnosis without exposing sensitive internal details. A well-designed error response might include the specific field that failed validation, the constraint that was violated, and the value that was rejected, enabling a client to highlight the offending input directly in a user interface. For server errors, a unique request identifier or trace ID included in the response allows support teams to correlate the client's report with server-side logs, dramatically reducing the time to resolution. This identifier should also be logged on the client side so that it can be included in support tickets without requiring the end user to capture it manually.

Beyond individual error responses, the API should provide feedback mechanisms for the operational health of the service as a whole. A dedicated health-check endpoint, potentially with varying levels of depth, enables load balancers and monitoring systems to determine whether the service is capable of handling requests. Rate-limiting information communicated through headers such as `X-RateLimit-Remaining` and `Retry-After` transforms an opaque 429 Too Many Requests response into a transparent signal that client code can use to implement backoff strategies, smoothing out traffic spikes and protecting the service from cascading failures.

Validation errors warrant particular care because they represent the most frequent point of friction during integration. Returning validation results as a collection—allowing multiple field-level errors to be reported in a single response—saves the client from the painful cycle of fixing one issue only to discover another. Each validation error should reference the specific location in the request body using a path notation such as JSON Pointer, describe the constraint that was violated, and where possible suggest a correction. This level of detail respects the developer's time and acknowledges that integration is a collaborative process between the API provider and the consumer, not an adversarial one.
---FINISH---

## Virtualization and Resource Abstraction

Cloud computing fundamentally relies on virtualization technologies that decouple physical hardware from computational workloads. Hypervisors such as KVM, Xen, and VMware ESXi partition physical servers into isolated virtual machines, each with its own operating system kernel and allocated resources. This abstraction enables multiple tenants to coexist on shared infrastructure without interference, forming the economic backbone of public cloud offerings. Modern cloud providers have extended this paradigm with hardware-assisted virtualization features like Intel VT-x and AMD-V, which reduce overhead by allowing guest operating systems to execute privileged instructions directly on the processor.

Containerization represents the next evolutionary step in resource abstraction. Unlike virtual machines, containers share the host operating system kernel while maintaining isolated user-space environments through Linux namespaces and cgroups. Docker popularized this approach, and Kubernetes has become the de facto orchestrator for managing containerized workloads at scale. The lighter footprint of containers enables density improvements of three to five times compared to traditional virtualization, substantially reducing infrastructure costs for microservice-based applications.

Beyond compute abstraction, cloud architectures virtualize networking and storage through software-defined networking (SDN) and software-defined storage (SDS) layers. SDN controllers dynamically provision virtual networks, subnets, and security groups programmatically, replacing manual switch configuration. Similarly, block, object, and file storage services abstract underlying disk arrays behind RESTful APIs. These abstractions collectively enable infrastructure-as-code practices where entire topologies are defined declaratively and provisioned automatically through orchestration tools like Terraform and CloudFormation.

## Distributed Systems and Scalability Patterns

Cloud-native applications must embrace distributed systems principles to achieve horizontal scalability. The shared-nothing architecture pattern eliminates single points of contention by ensuring each node operates independently with its own memory and storage. Stateless application servers paired with externalized state stores such as Redis or Amazon DynamoDB allow request routing to any available instance, facilitating elastic scale-out and scale-in operations. This pattern underpins the design of virtually all large-scale web services and API platforms running in production today.

Load balancing distributes incoming traffic across backend instances using algorithms ranging from simple round-robin to sophisticated least-connections and resource-aware scheduling. Layer 7 application load balancers inspect HTTP headers and paths to make routing decisions, enabling content-based traffic steering, A/B testing, and canary deployments. Global server load balancing extends these concepts across geographic regions, directing users to the nearest available data center based on latency measurements and health checks. Consistent hashing further optimizes distributed caching layers by minimizing cache invalidation when nodes join or leave the topology.

Data persistence in distributed architectures introduces well-known trade-offs formalized by the CAP theorem, which states that a distributed data store can simultaneously provide only two of consistency, availability, and partition tolerance. Cloud databases adopt different positions on this spectrum: Amazon Aurora prioritizes consistency through quorum-based replication, while Apache Cassandra favors availability with eventual consistency. Event-driven architectures using message brokers like Apache Kafka decouple producers from consumers, enabling asynchronous communication patterns that gracefully absorb traffic spikes and support backpressure mechanisms essential for system stability under load.

## Security and Resilience in Cloud-Native Design

The shared responsibility model delineates security obligations between cloud providers and customers. Providers secure the physical facilities, network infrastructure, and virtualization layer, while customers retain responsibility for operating system hardening, application security, identity management, and data encryption. Misunderstanding this boundary remains a leading cause of cloud security incidents. Organizations must implement defense-in-depth strategies that layer network security groups, web application firewalls, and runtime application self-protection across every tier of their cloud deployments.

Zero-trust architectures have emerged as the dominant security paradigm for cloud-native environments. Rather than assuming implicit trust based on network location, zero-trust models require continuous authentication and authorization for every access request. Mutual TLS encrypts service-to-service communication, while identity-aware proxies gate access to internal applications without requiring VPN connectivity. Secrets management services like HashiCorp Vault dynamically generate short-lived credentials, eliminating the risks associated with static API keys embedded in configuration files or source code repositories.

Resilience engineering treats failure as inevitable rather than exceptional. Chaos engineering practices deliberately inject faults into production systems to validate their behavior under degraded conditions. Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures by failing fast when downstream dependencies become unresponsive, while retry policies with exponential backoff and jitter avoid thundering herd problems during recovery. Multi-region active-active architectures replicate state across geographically distributed deployments, ensuring that the loss of an entire availability zone or region does not result in prolonged service disruption or permanent data loss.
<<<END>>
